title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, and Evidence Workflows
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's standards and operational procedures for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC controls, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and handling risk & exceptions. It is intended for engineers, security reviewers, product owners, and compliance teams responsible for secure design and evidence generation.

Key principles
- Principle of least privilege for all human and machine identities.
- Centralized, tamper-evident audit logging with immutable retention for compliance artifacts.
- Clear ownership and SLAs for evidence collection during audits and incidents.
- Documented, time-limited risk acceptances and exceptions with mandatory mitigation plans.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Summary
Redwood enforces role-based access control across control plane services (Console/API/CLI), infra management (Terraform, cloud consoles), and runtime admin planes (serving clusters). All access is authenticated via SSO (OIDC/SAML) for humans and short-lived credentials for service identities.

Role definitions (core)
- security-admin: Full access to security tooling, audit logs, policy management; two-person approval required for org-level policy changes.
- infra-admin: Manage cloud accounts, networks, and infra provisioning; no access to customer PII unless explicitly granted.
- platform-engineer: Deploy and operate runtime services, access to runtime metrics and traces; no IAM management by default.
- svc-account: Scoped machine identity for services, limited to specific APIs and roles via least privilege.
- developer: Read/write access to non-production projects, restricted production access via PR-based elevation.
- viewer: Read-only access to dashboards and runbooks.

Permission matrix (example - human readable)
| Resource | security-admin | infra-admin | platform-engineer | developer | viewer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Console:org-settings | Full | Read | Read | None | None |
| Audit logs | Full | Read | Read | None | Read |
| Deploy:production | Approve | Manage infra | Operate | Request only | None |
| Secrets:read | Scoped | Scoped | Scoped | None | None |

Authentication and onboarding
- All employees and contractors authenticate via SSO (Okta).
- New joiners are assigned a default role based on job function and must complete role-appropriate security training within 14 days.
- Service accounts are created through the service-account provisioning pipeline (owner: eng-infra) which requires a justification, expiry, and automated rotation schedule.

Elevation and emergency access
1. Developers request privileged production access via access request ticketing (Jira) citing scope and duration.
2. Requests auto-approve if policy satisfied (justification, recent code review, test coverage); otherwise require 2 approvers (owner + security).
3. Emergency elevation is logged as a high-priority audit event and requires retrospective review within 72 hours.

2) Audit Logging

Goals and scope
- Provide immutable, searchable audit trails for security-relevant actions across control plane, data plane, and infra.
- Preserve integrity and minimize blind spots (cloud console changes, KMS usage, account lifecycle events, runtime admin API calls).

Log sources and owners
- Console/API gateway (owner: eng-developer-experience) — user actions, API requests, admin operations.
- Identity provider (Okta) (owner: security) — login events, MFA changes, SSO config changes.
- Cloud provider IAM & org events (owner: eng-infra) — permission changes, role bindings.
- Serving runtime audit (owner: eng-serving-runtime) — model deployment events, rollback, KV cache invalidations.
- Key management (KMS/HSM) accesses (owner: security) — key usage records.

Retention and availability
- Audit logs: retained for 7 years (compliance default) and stored in region-specific immutable buckets.
- High-volume debug logs: retained 90 days by default and archived/rolled up after 90 days.
- Audit log SLO: 99.9% write availability for ingestion pipeline; alerts if ingestion lag > 5 minutes.

Tamper-evidence and integrity
- Logs are Write-Once (WORM) where supported; integrity hashes computed on ingest and stored separately.
- Regular integrity verification job (daily) validates hashes; failures open a security ticket and pager on-call.

Search, access, and review cadence
- Security and designated compliance reviewers have dedicated log search dashboards with export controls.
- Quarterly review of high-sensitivity logs (KMS, IAM changes) by security and biz-ops.

Sample query examples
- List all IAM role grants in the last 30 days: (console query) "event_type:iam.grant AND timestamp:>now-30d"
- KMS key usage by service: "resource.type:kms AND action:Encrypt* AND timestamp:>now-7d"

3) Data Residency & Retention

Residency controls
- Customer data categories are classified as: PII, Model Training Inputs, Evaluation Datasets, and Metadata.
- Customers can select residency region at onboarding: us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1. Data tagged with the region label must not leave the designated region for storage and backups.
- Cross-region replication for disaster recovery requires explicit customer opt-in and documented legal basis.

Encryption and key management
- All data at rest is encrypted with AES-256. KMS-backed keys are used per-region with customer-managed keys (CMKs) available for Private customers.
- Key rotation: CMKs rotated annually; service-managed keys rotated per cloud provider defaults.

Retention policy (defaults)
- Audit logs: 7 years (immutable).
- Model inference logs (non-PII): 90 days, aggregate analytics retained for 3 years.
- Customer PII: retention defined by contract; default retention 1 year unless otherwise specified.
- Backups: encrypted and retained for region-specific DR windows (30 days for ephemeral infra state, 365 days for customer snapshots if requested).

Data deletion and verification
- Deletion request workflow: ticket -> validation -> execution -> verification (cryptographic deletion proof or deletion confirmation log).
- Deletion verification log is retained for 1 year after deletion.

4) Secure SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle)

Controls required for all code shipped to production
- Pre-merge requirements: automated SAST, dependency SCA, unit test coverage threshold (>= 70% for security-sensitive modules), and at least one peer review.
- CI gating: failing security checks block merges. All pipeline failures create security tickets automatically.
- Build provenance: all production artifacts must include reproducible-build metadata and immutable artifact IDs.

Threat modeling and design review
- New services and protocol changes must complete a lightweight threat model and security design review (template in eng-platform/how-tos). High-risk changes require a formal architecture review board sign-off.

Secrets management and supply chain
- Secrets are never stored in repo; use vault-backed secrets with short-lived tokens.
- Third-party dependencies: maintain SBOM for all production services and update annually or on major upgrades.

Runtime protections
- Runtime sidecars enforce network egress policies and L7 allowlists.
- Canary rollout with verified telemetry and regression tests; automatic rollback on defined error budget breach.

5) Incident Response: Security Procedures

Detection and initial triage
1. Alerts from IDS/EDR, SIEM, or runtime monitors create a high-priority incident ticket.
2. First responder (on-call security engineer) performs initial triage within 15 minutes for high-severity events.

Containment and remediation steps (security-specific)
- Short-term containment: revoke compromised credentials, quarantine affected hosts/containers, and freeze deploy pipelines for implicated services.
- Preservation: enable forensic logging (increase log level and secure logs), take snapshots of affected systems, collect memory dumps if needed.
- Remediation: apply patches, rotate secrets, rebuild images from trusted CI artifacts.

Evidence handling and chain-of-custody
- Evidence artifacts (logs, disk images, memory captures) must be hashed on collection, uploaded to an evidence bucket with restricted ACLs, and recorded in the incident ticket.
- Chain-of-custody entry must include collector, timestamp, hash, and storage location.

Notifications and escalation
- Internal: notify leadership and affected teams within 60 minutes for Sev1 incidents.
- External/regulatory: follow the regulatory notification timelines (e.g., GDPR 72-hour breach notification) and consult Legal & Compliance for vendor/customer notifications.

Post-incident review
- Conduct a blameless postmortem within 7 business days. The postmortem must include root cause, timeline, mitigation actions, and evidence index.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Owners and evidence types
- Evidence owners are appointed per control domain (example: IAM controls -> eng-infra; Audit logging -> security).
- Typical evidence artifacts: access control matrices, IAM change logs, audit log exports, SAST/SCA reports, build provenance artifacts, penetration test reports, and policy attestation forms.

Evidence lifecycle and storage
- Evidence is stored in the compliance evidence repository (encrypted buckets with retention policy). Evidence items have metadata: evidence_id, owner, control_id, created_date, retention_until.
- Naming convention: EVID-<control>-<YYYYMMDD>-<owner initials> (e.g., EVID-IAM-20260210-MC).

Audit playbook (for external audits)
1. Intake: Compliance creates an audit package request listing controls and time windows.
2. Collection: Owners gather evidence and mark items in the repository.
3. Review: Security & Legal validate and annotate items; any gaps trigger remediation tickets.
4. Delivery: Package delivered via secure transfer (SFTP-or-encrypted-bundle) with delivery confirmation.
5. Retention: Evidence packaged for audit remains immutable for the audit-retention period (usually 7 years by default).

7) Risk and Exceptions

Exception request process
1. Submit an Exception Request (ticket) with: control impacted, justification, compensating controls, risk assessment, proposed expiry date, and owner.
2. Security review: Security and the control owner evaluate risk and propose mitigations or deny.
3. Approvals: For high-severity exceptions, require approval from Security Director and Product/Engineering Director.
4. Monitoring: Approved exceptions are tracked and reevaluated monthly until expiry.

Exception template (required fields)
- Exception ID
- Control(s) impacted
- Justification and business need
- Compensating controls (technical and procedural)
- Risk rating (Low/Medium/High)
- Proposed expiry and review cadence
- Approvers and reviewers

Risk acceptance guardrails
- Maximum exception duration: 90 days without executive waiver.
- No exceptions allowed for controls that protect customer encryption keys or key material unless signed off by Security Director and Legal.

C. Evidence checklist (quick)

- [ ] Audit log export for period
- [ ] SAST/SCA reports for services in scope
- [ ] Build provenance for production artifacts
- [ ] Incident chain-of-custody entries (if applicable)
